questions.stem: The Haber process uses a temperature of 450°C, 200 atm pressure, and an iron catalyst. The forward reaction (N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3) is exothermic. Why is 200 atm pressure used?

options.text: High pressure makes the catalyst work better
There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so high pressure shifts equilibrium right to produce more ammonia
High pressure is needed to liquefy the ammonia
High pressure increases the temperature of the reaction

questions.explanation: The left side has 4 moles of gas (1 N2 + 3 H2) and the right side has 2 moles (2 NH3). High pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer moles of gas (right), increasing ammonia yield. While even higher pressure would give more ammonia, 200 atm is a compromise - very high pressures require expensive equipment and pose safety risks.

questions.stem: In the Haber process, ammonia is continuously removed by cooling and liquefying it as it is produced. Why is this done?

options.text: To prevent the ammonia from decomposing at high temperature
To reduce the concentration of product, shifting equilibrium right and producing more ammonia
To keep the reactor at the correct temperature
Liquid ammonia is easier to store than gas

questions.explanation: By removing ammonia from the equilibrium mixture, the concentration of product decreases. Le Chatelier's principle tells us the equilibrium shifts to the right to replace the removed ammonia, producing more NH3. The unreacted N2 and H2 are recycled back into the reactor. This continuous removal is key to achieving high overall yield.

questions.stem: The Contact process produces sulfur trioxide: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), Delta H = -196 kJ/mol. A temperature of 450°C is used. Why not use a lower temperature for a higher yield?

options.text: Lower temperature would decompose the catalyst
A lower temperature gives higher yield but the reaction would be too slow, even with a catalyst
Lower temperature actually decreases the yield
The reaction does not occur below 450°C

questions.explanation: Since the forward reaction is exothermic, lower temperature would indeed shift equilibrium to the right, giving a higher yield of SO3. However, the rate would be too slow to be economically viable. 450°C with a vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5) catalyst is a compromise - giving about 99% conversion at an acceptable rate.

questions.stem: Ammonia produced by the Haber process is used to make nitric acid (HNO3) and then ammonium nitrate fertiliser. Why is the Haber process so important for global food production?

options.text: Ammonia is used directly as food for crops
Ammonia is converted into nitrogen-containing fertilisers that increase crop yields
The Haber process produces oxygen which plants need
Ammonia kills pests that damage crops

questions.explanation: The Haber process converts atmospheric nitrogen (which plants cannot use directly) into ammonia, which is then used to manufacture nitrogen-based fertilisers like ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3). These fertilisers provide essential nitrogen for plant growth, dramatically increasing crop yields. It is estimated that the Haber process supports food production for about half the world's population.

questions.stem: An industrial chemist wants to maximise the yield of ammonia. She suggests using 50 atm instead of 200 atm to reduce costs. What trade-off does this involve?

options.text: Lower pressure gives higher yield but slower rate
Lower pressure gives lower yield of ammonia but reduces equipment and energy costs
Lower pressure has no effect on yield or cost
Lower pressure gives higher yield because the catalyst works better

questions.explanation: Lower pressure means the equilibrium shifts less to the right (fewer moles side), giving a lower percentage yield of ammonia per pass. However, the equipment costs are much lower - high-pressure vessels and compressors are very expensive to build and maintain. The 200 atm compromise balances reasonable yield against manageable costs.
